questions.q: What gates does `PrepareGHZ` apply to produce its entangled state?
options: Three independent H gates with no entangling gates at all
Three CNOT gates with no Hadamard at all
A single measurement with no gates applied beforehand
One H gate on q0, followed by CNOT(q0,q1) and CNOT(q0,q2)
questions.explain: The GHZ-preparation circuit is H on the first qubit followed by CNOT from that qubit to each of the other two, entangling all three.

questions.q: According to the verified theoretical calculation, what is the probability of measuring the outcome ('Zero','One','Zero') from PrepareGHZ on an ideal simulator?
options: Exactly 0 -- this outcome has no amplitude at all in the theoretical GHZ state, which has nonzero amplitude only on |000> and |111>
Exactly 0.5
Approximately 0.125 (1 out of 8 equally likely outcomes)
It cannot be determined without running real hardware
questions.explain: Direct matrix computation of the 3-qubit state showed nonzero amplitude only on |000> and |111>, each with probability exactly 0.5; every other one of the 8 possible outcomes has probability exactly 0.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'the output looked reasonable' is a weak correctness check for this lab?
options: Because most wrong circuits also produce output that looks plausible at a glance -- only comparing empirical counts against an independently derived theoretical distribution catches the specific falsifiable claim about which outcomes are actually possible
Because this lab has no theoretical distribution to compare against
Because Python's Counter cannot display quantum results correctly
Because output never looks reasonable for quantum programs
questions.explain: A weak check (did it run, does it look plausible) can pass even for a buggy circuit. The real test is comparing against the specific, falsifiable theoretical prediction -- here, that only 000 and 111 are possible outcomes at all.

questions.q: In a 1000-shot run on an ideal, noiseless simulator, what counts would a CORRECT implementation of PrepareGHZ be expected to show?
options: Counts that cannot be predicted in advance under any circumstances
All 1000 shots landing on exactly one single outcome
Roughly even counts spread across all 8 possible 3-bit outcomes
Counts clustering near 500 for ('Zero','Zero','Zero') and near 500 for ('One','One','One'), with zero occurrences of any other outcome
questions.explain: Since only |000> and |111> have nonzero theoretical amplitude (each probability 0.5), a correct run should show roughly even counts split between those two tuples and exactly zero for any of the other six possible outcomes.

questions.q: If a small number of theoretically-impossible outcomes (like 010) appeared when running PrepareGHZ on real noisy hardware instead of a simulator, what would that most likely indicate, per the lesson?
options: Likely physical hardware noise, since real hardware doesn't guarantee the same theoretically-impossible-outcome exclusion a noiseless simulator does -- a different interpretation than seeing it on a simulator, which would point to a logic bug
A certain and obvious bug in the Q# code, identical to what it would mean on a simulator
That GHZ states cannot be prepared on real hardware under any circumstances
That Python's Counter object miscounted the results
questions.explain: On a noiseless simulator, a theoretically-impossible outcome appearing points to a code bug. On real noisy hardware, the same outcome appearing is expected to some degree due to physical noise -- a materially different diagnosis depending on which target produced the result.
